chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him: A man forgot the stoning (of the pillars) until he arrived in Mecca. He said: 'He returns and stones them, separating between each two throws by an hour.' I said: If he missed that and departed (from Mina), he said: 'There is no penalty upon him.'

I said: And a man forgot the Sa'i (walking) between As-Safa and Al-Marwah. He said: 'He repeats the Sa'i.' I said: If he missed that until he departed, he said: 'He returns and repeats the Sa'i. Indeed, this is not like the stoning of the pillars, for indeed the stoning is a Sunnah and the Sa'i between As-Safa and Al-Marwah is a Fard (obligatory duty).'

And we have also clarified in what preceded that standing at 'Arafat and Al-Mash'ar is obligatory, except that we do not exclude in this place what confirms what we have presented, and that which indicates that standing at 'Arafah is obligatory is what he narrated:

key_terms.اَلسَّعْيَ: The ritual walking between Safa and Marwah
key_terms.اَلْجِمَارَ: The stoning of the pillars in Mina

ai.seo_question: What is the difference in ruling between forgetting the stoning of the Jamarat and forgetting the Sa'i during Hajj?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the legal distinction between Sunnah and Fard rituals in Hajj, ruling that forgetting the stoning of Jamarat incurs no penalty if one departs, whereas missing the Sa'i requires returning to perform it. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential view that while Jamarat is a confirmed Sunnah, Sa'i is an obligatory pillar, a distinction reinforced by the explicit affirmation of the standing at 'Arafat as a Fard. The narration highlights the practical flexibility granted to pilgrims who forget rituals, contrasting the strictness of obligatory acts with the leniency of prophetic traditions.
